title: Comfort My People
sum: The book turns. After the long account of Assyria and Hezekiah, and the warning that Judah's treasures will be carried off to Babylon (39:6–7), a new voice opens with the word "Comfort". Jerusalem's hard service is over and her guilt paid. Voices call for a road through the desert so that the LORD can come home with his people, and a messenger is told to climb a mountain and announce to the towns of Judah, "Look, your God!" Human beings wither like grass, but God's word stands.

The rest of the chapter answers a tired people who say that God has lost track of them (40:27). Who measured the oceans, advised the Creator or made an idol worth comparing with him? The nations are a drop in the bucket; the stars come out at his call. The chapter ends with one of the Bible's best-known promises: those who wait for the LORD will get fresh strength and climb on their pinions like eagles.
readings: Read as a prophecy given in advance

Isaiah of Jerusalem looks past the exile he has just announced (39:6–7) and speaks comfort to those who will live through it. The opening 'Comfort' answers the closing threat of chapter 39, and the God who can name the future (41:21–29) is the God who sees his people's road (40:27).
Read as words to the exiles

A prophet in Babylon, about 545 BC, tells captives who have lived with defeat for forty years that the time of punishment is over. The heavenly council of chapter 6 meets again, and this time the order is not 'make their hearts fat' but 'speak to her heart'.
Read as the Gospel's opening

All four Gospels begin John the Baptist's work with 40:3. For Christian readers the voice in the wilderness announces the coming of the LORD in Jesus, and 'Look, your God!' (40:9) is fulfilled when he comes.

views.H: If the chapter is read against 539 BC, the 'road in the wilderness' is the way home from Babylon across the Syrian desert, which some exiles took after Cyrus's decree of 538 BC (Ezra 1). Babylon's own Processional Way, built by Nebuchadnezzar for the New Year festival of Marduk, is the background many see for the image of a god's highway.
views.C: Most critical scholars see 40:1–11 as the prologue of 'Second Isaiah' (40–55), a call scene in the divine council like 6:1–13 and 1 Kings 22:19–22 (Cross), in which the prophet's own commission is hidden in 40:6. The disputation of 40:12–31 answers the exiles' complaint with arguments from creation. Many also note how carefully the chapter is joined to the first half of the book, as if written to continue it (Williamson, Childs).
views.J: The synagogue reads 40:1–26 on Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath after the Ninth of Av, opening the seven haftarot of consolation. The Targum has 'Prophets, prophesy comfort to my people', and a midrash says that because Jerusalem sinned doubly and was punished doubly, she is comforted doubly (Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 16). Ibn Ezra hints that these chapters speak of the Babylonian exile.
views.X: Mark opens his Gospel with 40:3, and Matthew, Luke and John apply it to John the Baptist. 1 Peter 1:24–25 quotes 40:6–8 in the Greek form. Paul's question about who knew the Lord's mind (Romans 11:34; 1 Corinthians 2:16) is 40:13 in Greek. In Handel's Messiah the chapter supplies the first numbers: 'Comfort ye', 'Every valley', 'And the glory of the Lord', 'O thou that tellest good tidings to Zion' and 'He shall feed his flock'.
views.F: Readers who look for a future fulfillment note that 40:5 promises that 'all flesh' will see the LORD's glory together, which neither the return from Babylon nor the first coming of Jesus completed. They read the leveled valleys and mountains as the final appearing of God's glory to the whole world.

deep.b:
For Isaiah 40–44 the Plain is translated from the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), the basis of modern Hebrew Bibles, verse by verse from a word-for-word rendering. The Dead Sea Scrolls were read for every verse through the transcriptions of Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook (ETCBC dss): the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC, complete for these chapters), 1QIsa-b (1Q8), and the Cave 4 fragments 4QIsa-b (4Q56), 4QIsa-c (4Q57), 4QIsa-g (4Q61) and 4QIsa-h (4Q62), and the Cave 5 fragment 5QIsa (5Q3) at 40:16–19. The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus. The later correction in the Great Isaiah Scroll at 40:7–8 is described as reported by De Troyer and Herbison. Readings of the Targum (in Chilton's translation), of the Latin Vulgate and of Ziegler's critical Greek text are given as reported by those editions and the commentaries cited.

The variants list each place where the witnesses differ in meaning. Spelling differences, which are very common in the Great Isaiah Scroll, are not listed.

deep.h: Where the book turns: who wrote chapters 40–66?
deep.b:
Chapter 40 is where the question of Isaiah's authorship is decided for most readers. The book's opening pages treat it in full; here are the views as they bear on this chapter.

One prophet. Jewish and Christian tradition read the whole book as the work of Isaiah son of Amoz. Ben Sira (about 180 BC) says that Isaiah, with a great spirit, saw what would come at the end and comforted the mourners of Zion (Sirach 48:24–25), which is the language of 40:1 and 61:2–3. The Talmud says that Hezekiah's company wrote Isaiah down (Bava Batra 15a). The New Testament names Isaiah when it quotes chapters 40 and 53 (Matthew 3:3; John 12:38–41). No manuscript shows 40–66 as a separate book: the Great Isaiah Scroll copies the whole book as one, and its one visible break falls after chapter 33, not after 39 (reported by Longacre). Writers such as Oswald Allis, Edward J. Young, Alec Motyer and John Oswalt argue that the shared vocabulary of the two halves ('the Holy One of Israel', the highway, the remnant) points to one mind, and that a God who 'tells the end from the start' (46:10) can give a prophet words for a later generation. On this view the prophet who announced the exile in 39:6–7 was given its comfort too.

Two or three prophets. The medieval scholar Abraham ibn Ezra, on 40:1, cites Moses ha-Kohen Gikatilla on the return under Zerubbabel and hints that the chapters speak from the time of the exile. J. C. Döderlein (1775) and J. G. Eichhorn argued that 40–66 come from the exile, and Bernhard Duhm (1892) divided them into 'Second Isaiah' (40–55) and 'Third Isaiah' (56–66). Their reasons: Isaiah's name does not appear after chapter 39; Jerusalem is spoken of as already in ruins (44:26; 51:3); the hearers are in Babylon and are told to leave it (48:20); Cyrus is named as a living conqueror (44:28; 45:1); and the style changes. This is the view of most scholars today.

One book, many hands. Many recent scholars (Brevard Childs, Christopher Seitz, H. G. M. Williamson) stress that 40–66 were written to continue and complete 1–39: the council scene of 40:1–8 answers the call of 6:1–13, and the 'earlier things' of chapters 41–48 include the earlier prophecies of the book itself. Williamson argues that the prophet of the exile helped shape the first half.

This site does not decide the question. Each chapter page in 40–55 gives a traditional and a critical setting.

deep.h: A voice in the wilderness: Qumran and the Gospels
deep.b:
The Hebrew of 40:3 sets the wilderness with the road: 'A voice calls out: In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!' The Greek runs the words together, 'a voice of one calling in the wilderness', and the Gospels follow that wording (Matthew 3:3; John 1:23). So the Gospels place the voice in the desert, while the Hebrew places the road there.

About a century before John the Baptist, the Qumran community used the same verse to explain why it lived by the Dead Sea. Its Community Rule says that its members will separate from the wicked and go into the wilderness to prepare the way, 'as it is written', quoting 40:3 and writing the divine name as four dots; it explains the 'way' as the study of the law (1QS 8:12–16; compare 1QS 9:19–20). The community and the Gospels read the same verse of themselves, but in different ways: one by withdrawing to study, the other by announcing the one who was coming.

John the Baptist, a voice in the Judean desert near the Jordan, fits both the Greek and the Hebrew. Mark joins 40:3 to Malachi 3:1 and introduces both as 'Isaiah the prophet' (Mark 1:2–3); Luke extends the quotation through 40:5, ending with the Greek's 'salvation of God' (Luke 3:4–6).

settings.by: The LORD, with voices of his heavenly council, as the prophet hears them; the prophet himself answers in 40:6
settings.to: Those told to comfort (plural: heavenly attendants, prophets, or the prophet's circle), and through them Jerusalem and the people of Judah
settings.when: Debated: soon after the sentence of 39:6–7 in Hezekiah's reign, or about 545 BC as Cyrus rose
settings.why: To announce that Jerusalem's term of punishment is over and that God himself is coming to lead his people home, and to set that promise on a word that outlasts every human power. Whether the hearers were told of the exile in advance or were living in it, the oracle asks them to believe the promise before they can see it.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Isaiah's disciples and the faithful in Hezekiah's Judah, who had just heard that Babylon would carry off the royal house (39:6–7), are told that the exile will not be the end: God's covenant with Jerusalem will outlast it. Isaiah's words were sealed and written for a later day (8:16–17; 30:8), so that the exiles who lived it would have this comfort ready.

Exiles in Babylon about 545 BC, some forty years after Jerusalem fell, hear that their term of service is over. The call to build a road in the desert is a call to prepare for the journey home that Cyrus's rise was making possible.

settings.by: The prophet, speaking for the LORD (who speaks in the first person in 40:25)
settings.to: Jacob and Israel, who complain that the LORD has lost sight of them (40:27)
settings.why: To answer despair with argument. Questions about creation, the nations and idols lead to one conclusion: a God this great has not forgotten his people and does not tire. The aim is to turn the hearers' complaint into waiting in hope.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: For Judah under Assyrian pressure, and about to hear of Babylon (39:6–7), the argument says that empires are a drop in the bucket to the LORD, and it warns a nation tempted by its neighbors' images (40:18–20; compare 2:8, 20) that no idol can compare with him. The complaint of 40:27 is one Isaiah's own hearers could voice (compare 49:14), and the exiles later would.

Exiles who had watched Babylon's gods carried in procession and their own temple destroyed, and who concluded that the LORD had passed their case by, are shown that their God made the stars Babylon worshiped and gives strength to the tired.

title: The Gods on Trial
sum: God calls the far islands and their peoples to court. Who roused the conqueror from the east who tramples kings? While the nations' craftsmen nail their idols firm, God turns to Israel with some of the tenderest words in the Bible: 'you, Israel, my servant ... offspring of Abraham, who loved me'. Do not be afraid; I grip your right hand. Little 'worm' Jacob will become a threshing sledge, and the desert will grow cedars and flow with water.

Then the gods are put on trial. Let them tell what happened in the past or what will come, or simply do something, good or bad. They cannot. They are nothing, and their images are wind. The chapter introduces the themes of the next eight: the LORD alone knows and announces the future, and the conqueror he has raised up will turn out to be Cyrus.
readings: Read as a court scene

The chapter uses the forms of a trial: a summons (41:1), evidence (41:2–4), the defendants' silence (41:26–28) and a verdict (41:29). Between the two trials stand oracles of assurance for Israel, framed by 'Do not be afraid'. The court shows Israel that their God, not Babylon's, rules history.
Read as words of personal assurance

Readers through the centuries have taken 41:10 and 41:13 as God's promise to each believer in fear. The words were first spoken to the people as a whole, 'my servant', but they use the forms of a priest's answer to a single worshiper's lament.

views.H: The 'man from the east' who 'treads kings down' (41:2–3, 41:25) matches Cyrus's campaigns: he defeated the Median king Astyages (about 550 BC) and Croesus of Lydia (about 547 BC), and came from Persia, east of Babylon, and from Media in the north. Croesus's fall in particular shook the Greek 'islands' and coastlands of the west, which fits 41:5.
views.C: Form critics (Begrich, Westermann) identified two of Second Isaiah's basic forms here: the trial speech (41:1–7, 21–29) and the 'oracle of salvation', a promise beginning 'Do not be afraid' (41:8–13, 14–16), perhaps modeled on what a priest said to a worshiper after a lament. Assyrian prophecies to kings use the same 'Do not fear' formula (Parpola).
views.J: The Targum and Rashi read the man from the east in 41:2 as Abraham, whom God called from the east and who defeated kings (Genesis 14). Most Jewish commentators after Ibn Ezra read 41:25 of Cyrus. 41:8, Abraham 'who loved me', is the source of the title 'Abraham, God's friend' in Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition.
views.X: James 2:23 calls Abraham the friend of God, following 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7. Christian readers have taken the promises to 'Israel, my servant' as given to the church in Christ (Galatians 3:29), or as Israel's own promises that still stand (Romans 11:28–29); the churches differ (see below). 41:10 is one of the verses most often memorized by Christians.
views.F: Futurist readers expect the waters and trees of 41:17–20 to be fulfilled when Israel is restored in its land and the desert is renewed at the end of the age.

deep.h: "Do not be afraid": the oracle of salvation
deep.b:
In 1934 Joachim Begrich suggested that the repeated 'Do not be afraid' passages of Isaiah 40–55 (41:8–13, 41:14–16; 43:1–7; 44:1–5) borrow a form from worship. When a worshiper prayed a lament in the temple, a priest may have answered with a word from God: 'Do not be afraid ... I am with you ... I will help you.' Lamentations 3:57, 'You said, "Do not be afraid"', may echo such an answer. The form has three parts: an address with titles of honor ('Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen'), the assurance itself, and the reason, usually what God has already done.

Close parallels come from Assyria. In prophecies to Esarhaddon (680–669 BC), the goddess Ishtar of Arbela says to the king, 'Do not fear', and promises to stand by him and defeat his enemies (Parpola, Assyrian Prophecies). In Isaiah the same royal comfort is given to a captive people, not a king. This is part of a wider move in Isaiah 40–55: the promises once made to David's house are now addressed to the whole nation (55:3).

God calls Israel 'offspring of Abraham, who loved me' (41:8). The Hebrew 'ohavi is literally 'my lover', that is, 'the one who loved me' or 'my friend'. Jehoshaphat's prayer speaks of 'the offspring of your friend Abraham' (2 Chronicles 20:7), and James says that Abraham was named the friend of God (James 2:23). The title passed into Islam as Khalil Allah, 'the friend of God', and the Arabic name of Hebron, where Abraham's tomb is honored, is al-Khalil, 'the Friend'.

For the exiles the title made a point. Abraham had come from the same region they were now in, Ur and Harran (Genesis 11:31), and God had called him from 'the ends of the earth' (41:9). The God who chose one man from Mesopotamia had not rejected his family there.

settings.to: The islands and peoples of the far west, called as a court; the speech is meant for Israel to overhear
settings.when: Debated: written ahead by Isaiah, or spoken as Cyrus's conquests spread (550–539 BC)
settings.why: To ask who is behind a conqueror's rise. The nations answer only with panic and more idols; Israel is meant to see that the LORD, first and with the last, directs world events.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Judah in Hezekiah's day had seen Assyria trample nations and their gods (36:18–20; 37:12). Hearing that the LORD would raise up a still greater conqueror from the east told them that world history, including the empires that threatened them, was in his hand.
Exiles who had heard of Cyrus's victories over Media (about 550 BC) and Lydia (about 547 BC), which alarmed the western coastlands, are told that the LORD roused him.

settings.what: "Do not be afraid": oracles of assurance for Israel
settings.to: Israel, 'my servant', Abraham's descendants, small and fearful (41:14), poor and thirsty (41:17)
settings.why: To steady a frightened people while empires shake. God reminds them of their election, promises to hold them up, and pictures the desert transformed for them. 'You worm' and 'I grip your right hand' say where their strength lies: not in themselves but in the God who chose them.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: For a small kingdom that had just survived Sennacherib's siege and had been told of a coming exile, these words promise that God's choice of Abraham's family stands: 'I never rejected you' (41:9). The thirsty desert of 41:17–20 looks ahead to the road home.
For captives with no land, king or temple, 'I chose you, and I never rejected you' answers the fear that the exile meant the end of the covenant; the desert pictures the dangerous journey home.

settings.to: The gods of the nations, addressed directly; their worshipers and Israel are the audience
settings.why: To prove that the LORD alone is God by the test of prophecy: only he announced in advance what is now happening. The verdict, 'wind and emptiness', is aimed at Israelites tempted to think other gods had power.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: In Judah, where Ahaz had brought in foreign altars (2 Kings 16:10–16) and Manasseh would soon make idolatry official (2 Kings 21:1–9), the trial says that the gods of the great powers cannot even tell the future. The proof would come when the conqueror God foretold actually appeared.
Exiles surrounded by Babylon's diviners and its famous omen science, and tempted to think Marduk had defeated the LORD, are shown that only their God foretold Cyrus.

traditions.q: Who is "Israel, my servant" today: the Jewish people, the church, or both?
views: The church is the new people of God, but the Jews are not to be presented as rejected: God does not take back his gifts and call (Romans 11:29). Promises like 41:8–10 are read of Christ and the church, and still of Israel.

Calvin applies the promises to Israel in these chapters to the church, the spiritual offspring of Abraham, since all who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring (Galatians 3:29). Many later Reformed theologians, such as Charles Hodge and John Murray, add that Romans 11 foretells a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ, within the one church.
God's promises to the nation of Israel will be kept to that nation, including its restoration in the land. The church shares in Israel's spiritual blessings but does not replace Israel.

Many evangelicals outside the dispensational tradition, following historic premillennialists such as George Eldon Ladd, hold that the promises are fulfilled first in Christ, the true servant, and through him in one people of Jews and Gentiles, while Paul's hope for Israel's future (Romans 11:25–27) still stands.

title: My Servant, My Chosen One
sum: 'Look at my servant!' God presents a chosen figure on whom he has put his Spirit. He will bring justice to the nations, but quietly: he will not shout in the streets, snap a crushed reed or put out a dimly burning wick, and he himself will not burn dim until justice is firm on the earth. God, who stretched out the heavens, makes him a covenant of the people and a light to the nations, to open blind eyes and free prisoners.

A new song follows, in which the whole earth, from sailors to desert tribes, praises the LORD, who goes out like a warrior and cries out like a woman in labor to bring the new age to birth. The chapter ends sharply. The servant Israel is himself blind and deaf, looted and imprisoned, and he has not understood that it was the LORD who handed him over because he would not listen to his teaching.
readings: Read as the servant Israel

In 41:8 and 44:1 the servant is Israel. On this reading 42:1–9 describes Israel's calling to bring God's justice to the nations, and 42:18–25 shows how far Israel falls short of it. Rashi reads it this way, as did most earlier commentators according to Ibn Ezra, and so do some modern scholars.
Read as an individual

The servant of 42:1–4 acts gently, has a mission to the nations and is given 'as a covenant of the people', which seems to include Israel. Many readers therefore see an individual: the prophet (Ibn Ezra), Cyrus (Saadia Gaon, as Ibn Ezra reports), or the King Messiah (the Targum, Kimchi and Abarbanel).
Read of Jesus

Matthew quotes 42:1–4 in full of Jesus (Matthew 12:18–21), and the voice at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration echoes 42:1: 'in him I take delight' (Matthew 3:17; Matthew 17:5). Simeon's song, which calls the child a light that unveils God to the nations (Luke 2:32), takes up 42:6.

views.H: Read historically, the 'new things' of 42:9 are the events about to unfold around 539 BC: Babylon's fall and the exiles' release. Some scholars, noting 'in righteousness I have called you' in 42:6 and 45:13, have suggested that 42:1–7 was first spoken of Cyrus, the one who would release the prisoners; most think it describes a figure set apart from him.
views.C: Bernhard Duhm (1892) separated four 'servant songs' (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12) from their setting, arguing that they come from another hand. Many scholars now read them in context. Christopher North's survey (1948; 2nd ed. 1956) remains the classic account of the many identifications: collective, individual, and mixed.
views.J: The Targum adds 'the Messiah' to 42:1. The medieval commentators divide: Rashi reads the servant as Jacob, that is, Israel; Ibn Ezra reports that most commentators took him as the righteous of Israel and Saadia Gaon as Cyrus, and himself takes him as the prophet; Kimchi and Abarbanel read him as the King Messiah, Abarbanel expressly rejecting the other readings. Rabbinic tradition takes 42:21 as a verse in praise of the commandments (Mishnah Makkot 3:16).
views.X: For the New Testament, Jesus is this servant: gentle with the weak, filled with the Spirit, a light to the nations (Matthew 12:18–21; Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47). The church, as his body, is then called to share the servant's mission (in Acts 13:47 Paul and Barnabas apply Isaiah 49:6 to themselves).
views.F: Readers who look ahead note that 42:4, 'until he sets justice firm on the earth', has not yet been completed, and take it as a promise for the return of Christ.

deep.b:
The question has been asked since the Ethiopian official asked Philip about another servant passage: 'The prophet says this of whom? Of himself, or of someone else?' (Acts 8:34). The main answers for 42:1–9 are these.

Israel. In the chapters on either side the servant is Israel by name (41:8–9; 44:1–2, 21), and the Greek writes 'Jacob' and 'Israel' into 42:1. The nation is chosen to make God's justice known. Against this, the servant here has a mission to 'the people' (42:6), apparently Israel itself, and in 42:18–25 Israel is the blind servant who needs the help this servant gives.

The faithful within Israel, or an ideal Israel: the servant is the people as they are called to be, and the 'blind servant' is Israel as it is.

An individual: the prophet himself; a coming king (the servant 'brings out justice', a royal task, and receives the Spirit, like the shoot of Jesse in 11:1–4); or Cyrus. Saadia Gaon proposed Cyrus, and Ibn Ezra the prophet himself. The Targum, Kimchi and Abarbanel make him the King Messiah, while Rashi reads Israel.

Jesus. Matthew 12:18–21 quotes the whole song as fulfilled in Jesus' quiet healing ministry, and the Gospels' baptism voice echoes 42:1.

Many interpreters combine these: the servant is Israel, but the task is so great that it is focused in one person who does what the nation could not. The servant topic page gathers the evidence across 40–55.

The phrase 'or goyim, 'a light to the nations', appears in 42:6 and again in 49:6, where the servant's task of restoring Israel is called 'too small' and he is made a light 'so that my salvation reaches the end of the earth'. It is one of the clearest statements in the Hebrew Bible that Israel's God intends blessing for every people (compare Genesis 12:3). The New Testament takes it up for Jesus (Luke 2:32, Simeon's song; John 8:12) and for the church's mission to the Gentiles (Acts 13:47; Acts 26:23).

The phrase has also been widely used in modern Jewish thought for Israel's moral calling among the nations.

settings.what: The first servant song and God's word to the servant
settings.by: The LORD, presenting his servant (42:1–4) and then addressing him (42:5–9)
settings.to: An unnamed audience, perhaps the heavenly council or the nations, in 42:1–4; the servant himself in 42:5–9; and Israel, who overhears
settings.when: Debated, as for the rest of 40–55
settings.why: To announce God's chosen agent and the gentle way he will bring justice. For a people crushed like a reed and dim like a wick, the song promises that God's justice will not break them further; 42:8 insists that the glory belongs to the LORD alone.
settings.readers: The returned community, which still awaited the justice promised here, and later readers who asked who the servant was: Israel, a prophet, or the Messiah (the Targum), and, for the New Testament, Jesus (Matthew 12:18–21).
views: Isaiah's hearers had been promised a just king from David's line on whom the Spirit would rest (9:6–7; 11:1–5). This song describes God's servant in the same terms, with a mission reaching the nations, and set the hope of Hezekiah's Judah beyond any king they knew.

A prophet among the exiles in the 540s BC presented a servant figure, whom he may have understood as Israel, a faithful group within it, or himself; for exiles the song promised that God's justice would reach even the nations that held them.

settings.what: A new song: the LORD goes out as a warrior
settings.by: The prophet, calling the world to praise; the LORD speaks in 42:14–17
settings.to: The whole earth, from the sea to the desert towns of Kedar and Sela; Israel hears it as a call to join
settings.why: To celebrate in advance the victory God is about to win, as Israel sang after the exodus (Exodus 15). The hymn gives the hearers words for a deliverance they have not yet seen, and warns idolaters that they will be put to shame.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Judah, which worshiped at the temple where new psalms were sung (compare Psalm 96; Psalm 98), is given a new song for a victory still to come, and is told that God's long silence (42:14) will end.
Exiles who asked how they could sing the LORD's song 'on foreign soil' (Psalm 137:4) are given a new song for the deliverance about to begin.

settings.by: The LORD, with the prophet's voice joining in 42:24 ('we sinned')
settings.to: Israel, the servant who has eyes and ears but does not understand
settings.when: Debated; the hearers are described as looted and shut away in jails
settings.why: To explain disaster: the plundering of Israel was not the defeat of Israel's God but his judgment on a people who refused his teaching. The accusation clears the way for the promise of 43:1; only a people who understand why they suffered can hear 'Don't be afraid'.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Isaiah had been told that the people would see and not understand (6:9–10), and his hearers had already seen the northern kingdom deported and Judah's towns looted by Assyria (1:7–8). The passage tells them, and the exiles after them, that such losses come from the LORD's hand.
Exiles, plundered and imprisoned, who asked how this could happen to the LORD's people, are told plainly: 'Wasn't it the LORD, the one we sinned against?'

title: You Are My Witnesses
sum: 'But now': straight after the accusation of 42:18–25 comes one of the Bible's warmest promises. The God who created and shaped Israel has redeemed them and called them by name. Through water and fire he will be with them; he would give whole nations in exchange for them, and he will gather his sons and daughters from every direction.

Then a courtroom again. The nations are asked to produce witnesses who foretold these events; Israel, blind and deaf as it is, is God's witness that 'I am he' and that there is no savior but him. God is about to do something new, a road through the wilderness greater than the road through the sea. The chapter ends with a final charge: Israel did not honor God with its worship, but wearied him with its sins, and yet he is the one who wipes them out 'for my own sake'.
readings: Read as a new exodus

The chapter retells the exodus: water that does not drown (43:2), Egypt as a ransom (43:3), a road in the sea (43:16–17) and water in the desert (43:19–20). The return from Babylon is pictured as a second exodus so great that the first can be forgotten (43:18).
Read as a trial

The two trials (43:8–13 and 43:22–28) frame the new exodus. In the first, Israel testifies for God against the nations; in the second, God takes Israel to court for its sins. Both end in the same truth: God saves for his own name's sake, not because of his witnesses' merit.

views.H: Babylon's ships (43:14) traded and fought on the Euphrates and the Persian Gulf. Cyrus's son Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BC; some read 43:3, 'I hand over Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba to take your place', as foreseeing Persia's gains in Africa in exchange for releasing Israel. The return was smaller than the gathering 'from the sunrise ... from the sunset' (43:5–6), which some take as hyperbole and some as still to come.
views.C: Critical scholars see in 43:16–21 the clearest statement of the 'new exodus' theme of 40–55, and in 43:22–28 a reply to exiles who protested that they had kept up their worship. The lack of sacrifices in 43:23 is read by some as a sign that the temple lay in ruins.
views.J: The midrash Sifre on Deuteronomy (346) cites 43:12, 'You are my witnesses ... I am God', and says: when you are my witnesses, I am God; when you are not, I am not God, as it were. The haftarah for Vayikra (Leviticus 1) is 43:21–44:23, matching the theme of offerings.
views.X: Christian readers hear 43:1–3 at baptisms ('when you cross the water, I am with you') and read 43:19 of the new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17; Revelation 21:5). 'You are my witnesses' (43:10) lies behind Jesus' charge to the apostles to be his witnesses (Acts 1:8). Jehovah's Witnesses took their name from 43:10–12 in 1931.
views.F: Futurist readers expect a final regathering of Jews from every direction (43:5–6) and see the modern return to the land as its beginning or as a sign of it.

deep.b:
In 43:8–13 the LORD convenes a world court. The nations are invited to bring witnesses who can prove that their gods foretold anything; they bring none. Then God calls his own witnesses, and they are a surprising choice: the people just described as blind and deaf (42:18–19; 43:8). They are witnesses not because they understood but because they experienced what God foretold and did: 'It was I who told it, I who saved' (43:12). Their very survival is the evidence.

The words have had a long life. The rabbis drew from 43:12 the daring saying that God's being God depends, 'as it were', on Israel's witness (Sifre Deuteronomy 346). Jesus tells his followers that they will be his witnesses (Acts 1:8), and the Greek martys, 'witness', becomes the word 'martyr'. In 1931 the Bible Students associated with the Watch Tower Society took the name Jehovah's Witnesses from 43:10–12.

Isaiah 40–55 often pictures the return from Babylon as a second exodus: a road in the wilderness (40:3; 43:19), water from the rock (48:21), the LORD going before and behind (52:12). Chapter 43 is the center of the theme. God is introduced as the one 'who opened a road in the sea' and drowned Pharaoh's chariots like a snuffed wick (43:16–17), and then says, 'Stop calling the earlier things to mind' (43:18). The new deliverance will be so great that even the exodus pales beside it. Jeremiah makes the same comparison (Jeremiah 16:14–15; Jeremiah 23:7–8).

The New Testament takes up the pattern: John the Baptist prepares the wilderness road, and Jesus' death is called his 'exodus' (Luke 9:31, in Greek). The new song and new creation of Revelation (Revelation 15:3; Revelation 21:5) close the theme.

settings.what: "You belong to me": an oracle of assurance
settings.by: The LORD, creator and redeemer of Israel
settings.to: Jacob and Israel, scattered and afraid
settings.when: Debated, as for the rest of 40–55
settings.why: To answer the accusation of 42:18–25 with grace: 'But now'. The oracle tells the people that they still belong to God by creation, redemption and name, and that he will bring the scattered home from every direction.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: For Judah, which had seen the northern tribes scattered by Assyria in 722 BC and had been warned of its own exile, the promise to gather sons and daughters from north and south, east and west, reaches all Israel's scattered people.
For exiles who had lost land, king and temple, the oracle says that they are still God's, and that the scattered Judeans in Babylon, Egypt and elsewhere will be gathered.

settings.what: The court of the nations: "You are my witnesses"
settings.to: The assembled nations as the court; Israel as God's witness
settings.why: To prove the LORD's sole deity by the evidence of prophecy fulfilled and salvation given. Israel learns that its role is not to win the case but to testify to what God has done.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Judah had just seen God save Jerusalem from Sennacherib as Isaiah foretold (37:33–37). It is called to be a witness that the LORD alone tells the future and saves, a testimony that would carry it through the exile to come.
Exiles, blind and deaf as they are, are called to testify that their God foretold the events now unfolding with Cyrus, while Babylon's gods said nothing.

settings.what: A road in the wilderness: the new exodus
settings.by: The LORD, 'your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel'
settings.to: Israel, about Babylon and its fall
settings.when: Debated; Babylon is named as the power about to fall
settings.why: To announce Babylon's fall and Israel's release as a new exodus, and to tell the hearers to look forward rather than back. The promise of water in the desert answers the fear of a dangerous journey home.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: In Hezekiah's day Babylon was a rebel city courting Judah (39:1–2), not yet an empire. Telling Judah that the LORD would bring Babylon down and lead his people out of it set the coming exile inside a larger story, a second exodus.
Captives in Babylon hear that their captor will fall and that the road home will be like the road through the sea, only greater.

settings.what: A trial against Israel: not offerings, but sins
settings.to: Jacob and Israel, who may have felt they had served God faithfully
settings.when: Debated; the charge fits corrupt worship before the exile or its absence in exile
settings.why: To strip away any claim that Israel had earned its rescue, so that the forgiveness of 43:25 is seen as pure grace. The trial explains the judgment ('I handed Jacob over to the ban') and makes room for the promise that follows in 44:1.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Isaiah had already condemned Judah's busy but empty sacrifices (1:10–15). Here the same people are told that their offerings were never really for God, and that his forgiveness would not depend on them.

Exiles who could not sacrifice at all, and perhaps protested that they had been faithful, are told that their sins, not neglected rites, brought the exile, and that God wipes them out for his own sake.

title: No God but Me
sum: God pours water on dry ground and his Spirit on Israel's children; people will gladly write 'Belongs to the LORD' on their hands. Then he declares, 'I am first, and I am last, and except for me there is no god', and asks who else can tell the future. Between these claims and the call to remember stands the Bible's longest satire on idols: the ironworker who grows faint making a god, the carpenter who carves a handsome human figure, and the man who cooks supper with half a log and prays to the other half, 'Rescue me! You are my god.'

The chapter ends with forgiveness ('Like a thick cloud I have wiped away your rebellions'), a call for all creation to sing, and a long description of God as maker of all things, the one who confirms his prophets' words. Its last word is a name: God says of Cyrus, 'My shepherd! He will do all that I please', and promises that Jerusalem and its temple will be rebuilt.
readings: Read as prophecy naming its fulfiller

On the traditional reading, 44:28 is the climax of the argument of chapters 41–48: God proves he alone is God by naming, about 150 years in advance, the king who would let the exiles go. Josephus says Cyrus himself read this passage.
Read as words in Cyrus's lifetime

On the critical reading, the prophet names a king whose victories his hearers were following. The claim is not that the name is predicted but that God planned and announced Cyrus's work through earlier prophecy (41:2, 25; 44:26), and now reveals that the conqueror is his chosen instrument for Israel.
Read as an argument against idols

Whatever its date, the chapter contrasts the God who makes everything (44:24) with the gods that people make (44:9–20). The satire works by showing the idol-maker's own logic: the same tree warms him, feeds him and is worshiped by him.

views.H: Cyrus took Babylon in October 539 BC; the Nabonidus Chronicle says his army entered 'without a battle'. In his first year as king of Babylon (538) he allowed the Judeans to return and rebuild the temple (Ezra 1:1–4; Ezra 6:3–5). The foundations were laid soon after (Ezra 3:10), and the temple was finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt only under Nehemiah, about 445 BC.
views.C: For most critical scholars the naming of Cyrus is the clearest sign that 40–55 date from the 540s BC. Some think 'Cyrus' in 44:28 and 45:1 may be an editor's gloss explaining the anonymous conqueror of 41:2 and 41:25, but most take it as original. 44:9–20 is often thought to be a separate prose satire set into the poems.
views.J: The haftarah for Vayikra ends at 44:23. Jewish tradition, including Josephus and the rabbis, accepts that Isaiah named Cyrus in advance; Ibn Ezra's comments on these chapters were taken by later scholars as hinting at a later author.
views.X: Revelation gives the title 'the First and the Last' (44:6) to the risen Jesus (Revelation 1:17; Revelation 2:8; Revelation 22:13), a key text in the doctrine of Christ's deity. Paul's critique of idolatry in Romans 1:22–25 and his speech in Athens (Acts 17:24–29) follow the logic of 44:9–20. Some Christian writers have read Cyrus, the deliverer called by name and 'anointed' (45:1), as a type of Christ.
views.F: Some futurist readers see in the Spirit poured out on Israel's children (44:3) a promise still awaiting fulfillment in a national turning of Israel to God at the end of the age, connected with Joel 2:28–29 and Zechariah 12:10.

deep.h: Cyrus named: the strongest case for each view
deep.b:
44:24–28 and 45:1–7 name Cyrus II of Persia, who took Babylon in 539 BC. Isaiah son of Amoz was active about 740–700 BC. How readers account for the name decides much else about chapters 40–66. Here each view is given in its strongest form.

The traditional view: a prediction about 150 years in advance. (1) The passage presents itself as prediction, and as the proof of God's claim. The whole argument of chapters 41–48 is that the LORD, unlike the idols, 'tells the end from the start' (46:10); he challenges the gods to 'tell us the things to come' (41:23), and then names his instrument. If the name were added after the event, the proof would be empty. (2) The Bible has another named prediction: a man of God names Josiah about three centuries before him (1 Kings 13:2). (3) Josephus records that Cyrus read his name in Isaiah's book and was moved by it to free the Jews (Jewish Antiquities 11.5–6); Ezra 1:2 has Cyrus say that the LORD 'has appointed me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah', the very task of 44:28. (4) There is no manuscript of chapters 40–66 apart from 1–39, and early tradition, Jewish and Christian, knew only one Isaiah (Sirach 48:24–25; John 12:38–41). (5) For those who believe God can reveal the future, the critical objection that prediction of names is impossible assumes what it should prove. (Allis, Young, Oswalt, Motyer.)

The critical view: a prophet in Cyrus's day. (1) The prophets of the Bible usually speak to their own generation about events within its horizon, and these chapters assume their hearers' situation: Jerusalem in ruins and waiting to be rebuilt (44:26), Babylon still standing, the exiles told to leave it (48:20). (2) Cyrus appears not as a distant figure but as someone already on the march, whose victories the hearers can see (41:2–3, 25); 'Who has roused a man from the east?' assumes he is known. (3) The point of the argument from prophecy is that God announced beforehand what is now taking place, the 'earlier things' (41:22; 48:3–6), including the older prophecies of Babylon's fall in Isaiah 13–14 and 21; this argument works best if the prophet stands at the moment of fulfillment. (4) Isaiah's name, and the kings of his time, disappear after chapter 39, and the style and vocabulary change. (5) 1 Kings 13:2 is itself widely thought to be shaped after Josiah's reform. On this reading the prophet's claim is no less bold: that the LORD, not Marduk, called Cyrus (compare the Cyrus Cylinder, in which Marduk calls out Cyrus's name for kingship), and that he did so for Israel's sake. (Duhm, Westermann, Blenkinsopp, Paul.)

Some scholars combine these, holding that the book was designed as one work and that the exilic prophet saw himself as continuing Isaiah's vision (Childs, Seitz, Williamson). The book's opening pages discuss authorship as a whole.

deep.h: The idol-maker: satire and ancient worship
deep.b:
The satire of 44:9–20 follows the making of an image step by step: the smith who forges a tool until he is faint with hunger, the carpenter who measures, marks, shapes and gives it human form, and the man who plants a tree, waits for rain, burns half of it to bake bread and roast meat, and bows to the rest. The punch line is that he 'cannot rescue his own life or say, "This thing in my right hand is a lie, isn't it?"' (44:20).

Babylonian worshipers would have replied that the statue was not the god. A new statue was brought to life by the 'mouth washing' and 'mouth opening' rituals, in which the craftsmen solemnly denied having made it and the god was invited to dwell in it (Walker and Dick). The satire deliberately ignores that defense. From the prophet's standpoint, a god whose body has to be manufactured, nailed down and carried (46:1–2, 7) is no god. The same argument appears in Jeremiah 10:1–16, Psalm 115:4–8, the deuterocanonical Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–19 and the Letter of Jeremiah, and the early church used it against Roman religion.
deep.refs: 40:18–20; 41:6–7; 44:9–20; 46:1–7; Jeremiah 10:1–16; Psalm 115:4–8; Wisdom of Solomon 13:10–19; Letter of Jeremiah; Romans 1:22–25; Acts 17:29

echoes: 40:18–20; 41:2–4; 41:25; 42:5; 45:1–7; 45:13; 46:1–11; 48:12–15; Deuteronomy 4:28; Deuteronomy 32:4; Deuteronomy 32:15; Deuteronomy 33:26; 1 Kings 13:2; 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–4; Ezra 3:10–13; Ezra 6:15; Psalm 115:4–8; Jeremiah 10:1–16; Joel 2:28–29; John 7:37–39; Acts 2:17; Acts 17:24–29; Romans 1:22–25; Revelation 1:17; Revelation 2:8; Revelation 22:13

settings.what: "My Spirit on your children": an oracle of assurance
settings.to: Jacob, 'my servant', and Jeshurun, the people God chose
settings.when: Debated, as for the rest of 40–55
settings.why: To follow the verdict of 43:28 with a promise for the next generation: God's Spirit will make them flourish, and people will be proud to bear the LORD's name.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: For Judah, told that its own sons would be carried off (39:7), the promise is that their children will flourish by God's Spirit and gladly claim the names Jacob and Israel.
Exiles who feared that their children would be absorbed into Babylon hear that the next generation, and even foreigners, will take Israel's name with pride.

settings.what: "No god but me": a trial speech
settings.by: The LORD, 'the King of Israel, its redeemer, the LORD of Armies'
settings.to: Any rival god, challenged to speak; Israel, addressed as witness (44:8)
settings.why: To restate the case of 41:21–29 and 43:8–13 in its sharpest form: the LORD is first and last, foretold the future, and knows of no other rock, so Israel need not panic before other gods.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Judah, surrounded by the gods of Assyria and its neighbors, is told: 'Is there a God apart from me?' The LORD had told them long ago, and they are his witnesses.
Exiles faced with the splendor of Babylon's gods are told that their God alone was there first and will be there last.

settings.by: The prophet (no 'the LORD says' introduces it)
settings.to: Israel, about the makers and worshipers of images
settings.when: Debated; many think it was written separately and set into the poems
settings.why: To make idolatry ridiculous by describing only what the craftsmen do. Laughing at the idol-maker frees the hearers from awe of what he makes.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: In Judah, where images were common and Manasseh would soon set a carved idol of Asherah in the temple itself (2 Kings 21:7), the satire told the faithful that the gods of their neighbors, and of their own rulers, were blocks of wood.

A prophet among the exiles, or a later writer of the same school, faced with Babylon's great images and festivals, mocks them for captives tempted to be impressed; the piece may first have stood on its own.

settings.what: "Remember this, Jacob" and a hymn of praise
settings.by: The LORD (44:21–22) and the prophet, calling creation to sing (44:23)
settings.to: Israel, and the heavens, the depths, the mountains and the forest
settings.why: To draw the lesson of the satire ('Keep these things in mind') and announce forgiveness before any repentance is asked: 'I have wiped away ... Turn back to me.' The hymn gives the hearers words of praise for a redemption God speaks of as already done.
settings.readers: The returned community in Persian Yehud, who read these words beside the small and difficult rebuilding of Ezra 1–6, and later the synagogue, which reads much of chapters 40–44 as haftarot of consolation.
views: Judah under judgment is told that God has already decided to forgive and redeem; the call 'Turn back to me' is the call Isaiah had made from the start (1:16–18; 31:6).
Exiles who saw their captivity as proof of unforgiven sin hear that the sins are gone like a morning cloud, and that they can return to God before they return home.

settings.by: The LORD, Israel's redeemer and maker of all things
settings.to: Israel; the oracle continues in 45:1–7, addressed to Cyrus himself
settings.when: The central question of the book's authorship: about 700 BC, or the 540s BC (see the section above)
settings.why: To show that the LORD who made the world also directs its rulers: he overturns diviners, confirms his prophets, and names the king who will rebuild Jerusalem and its temple. The naming is the climax of the argument from prophecy in chapters 41–48.
settings.readers: The returned community, who saw Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:1–4) and the founding of the temple (Ezra 3:10) as the fulfillment of this oracle, and later readers, Jewish and Christian, for whom it became the book's central question of date.
views: Isaiah of Jerusalem, about 700 BC, named Cyrus some 150 years ahead. For Hezekiah's Judah it was a promise that the city and temple Babylon would destroy would be rebuilt; for the exiles it would be the proof that only the LORD foretells the future. Josephus says Cyrus later read the passage.

A prophet among the exiles in the 540s BC named the Persian king already advancing on Babylon and declared him the LORD's chosen instrument, so that the hearers would see Persia's rise as God's work for them.

traditions.q: Revelation gives the LORD's title "I am first, and I am last" (44:6) to Jesus. Does that make Jesus the God of Israel?
views: Yes. Jesus is 'true God from true God', one in being with the Father. The New Testament gives Jesus the title 'Lord', the Greek rendering of the divine name, and Revelation's use of 44:6 for him belongs to the same confession.

Yes. Christ is the eternal Word who spoke in Isaiah; Orthodox icons write 'the one who is' (Ho On, the Greek of Exodus 3:14) in his halo. The Son shares the one divine nature with the Father and the Spirit.

Yes. Many evangelical scholars argue that Revelation deliberately includes Jesus within the unique identity of Israel's one God, since 44:6 is a claim that no one else is God, and Revelation 22:13 sets the title beside 'the Alpha and the Omega'.

No. In Isaiah the title belongs to Jehovah alone, in the sense that there is no God before or after him. When Jesus calls himself 'the First and the Last' in Revelation 1:17–18 and 2:8 he means something different: he was the first human raised to immortal spirit life and the last to be raised by Jehovah himself.
Yes, in their own sense: Jesus Christ is Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament, who spoke through the prophets; he is a divine being distinct from God the Father.
